newsitem.title: USA: NYS gov gets pact to examine Swiss banks' records.
newsitem.headline: NYS gov gets pact to examine Swiss banks' records.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki on Thursday said he had reached a pact with the Swiss Federal Banking Commission that lets state examiners go over records of the nation's banks that are in Switzerland.
The probe is part of an effort to get to the bottom of whether Swiss banks held onto unclaimed bank accounts of Holocaust victims and stonewalled some of their efforts to track down assets.
"The accord marks the first time a governmental agency outside of Switzerland will be allowed to review Holocaust-related documents from this era, on their soil," Pataki said, in prepared comments.

The accord between New York State and Switzerland's bank regulators comes on the heels of the country's creation on Wednesday of a Jewish-Swiss humanitarian fund for Holocaust victims, which was hailed by Jewish leaders as "historic."

Based on the recommendation of the World Jewish Congress, the New York State comptroller, H. Carl McCall, then lifted a ban on putting the state's excess cash to work at Swiss banks in the form of short-term investments. New York State was the only state to bar Swiss banks in such a manner.
The Pataki Administration sent its banking superintendent, Neil Levin, to Switzerland earlier this month to meet with officials from the Swiss Bank Corp, Union Bank of Switzerland, and Credit Suisse.

The new accord that was negotiated between the state and the Swiss Federal Banking Commission lets New York State bank examiners review confidential customer information about dormant accounts and any other previously classified materials about unclaimed assets that were held in New York, according to the governor's prepared statement.
The Swiss Federal Banking Commission is the main regulator of the Swiss operations of these banks.

The Swiss Bank set up a New York office in 1939, followed by Credit Suisse in 1940. The agreement covers the accounts of Holocaust victims that were held in branches or agencies of Swiss banks in New York, and New York institutions that acted as correspondent banks for the Swiss banks from 1933 to 1945.

Accounts that might have been transferred to Switzerland before 1960 also are covered by the pact, according to a letter to the New York Superintendant of Banks from the Swiss Federal Banking Commission.
